extracted.intended_audience: employers, employee advocates, labor lawyers, State officials, policymakers, and other stakeholders participating in DOL rulemaking on overtime/EAP exemptions
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and decision criteria for selecting and justifying a standard salary level to pair with the EAP duties test in the Department of Labor's overtime regulations. Focuses on methodology (percentiles/region/contemporaneous data), historical consistency, legal defensibility, and the salary level's screening function.

rubrics_metrics.name: Restore the salary level's screening function
rubrics_metrics.description: The salary level test must equal at least the long test salary level in order to fulfill its historical screening function: "the salary level test must equal at least the long test salary level ..." and ensure employees who were nonexempt because they earned less than the long-test or long-test-equivalent salary level are also nonexempt under the standard test.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Department reaffirms that fully effectuating the salary level's screening function is key to setting an appropriate dividing line. Using current data, achieving this objective requires a standard salary level amount at least equal to the long test level (the NPRM cited $942 per week using current data, roughly the 25th percentile in the South). The Department estimates restoring the screening function at that level would affect approximately 1.8 million employees who currently earn between the existing standard ($684) and the long-test level ($942). Historical practice (1938–2019) excluded salaried white-collar employees below the long-test level from the exemption based on salary alone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Account for the shift from a two-test to a one-test system
rubrics_metrics.description: Methodology should account for the 2004 shift from a two-test (long and short duties tests with two salary levels) to a single standard duties test, which altered how nonexempt work is evaluated and broadened the exemption.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Department recognizes a single-test system is inherently less nuanced than a two-test system (two salary levels and two duties tests vs. one of each). Any salary-level methodology should seek to mitigate the one-test system's loss of precision—e.g., by restoring protections to lower-salaried employees historically protected by the long duties test—while accepting that no single salary level can perfectly replicate the two-test system. Options include increasing the salary level or reinstating a more rigorous duties limitation, but the Department did not propose returning to a two-test system.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use contemporaneous earnings data and clear percentile/region methodology
rubrics_metrics.description: Set the salary level based on contemporaneous labor-market earnings data, typically using a specified percentile of weekly earnings of full-time salaried workers in a designated region (e.g., the lowest-wage Census Region, the South).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Different rulemakings have used different percentiles and regions: the 2016 rule used the 40th percentile in the South (producing $913/week), the NPRM proposed the 35th percentile in the lowest-wage Census Region, and commenters proposed applying the 2004/2019 methodology (20th percentile in the South or retail nationally). The selection of percentile and region directly affects the resulting salary threshold and who is screened out by salary alone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid making the salary level determinative for too many individuals
rubrics_metrics.description: Design the salary-level methodology so that the salary test does not 'disqualify any substantial number of bona fide executive, administrative, and professional employees' or otherwise become the de facto sole determinant of exemption status.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This concern motivated criticism of the 2016 rule; commenters warned against a salary-only approach that excludes many employees who legitimately meet the duties test. The Department must balance restoring protections for lower-paid workers who perform substantial nonexempt work against overbroad exclusion of bona fide EAP employees. The Department frames beneficial distributional effects as byproducts, not the statutory basis for choosing a level.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ensure the salary level complements, not replaces, duties analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: The exemption 'should turn on an analysis of [employees'] actual functions, not their salaries,' meaning the salary level serves primarily as an initial screening device while the duties test determines bona fide EAP status.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Department emphasizes that the salary level is a 'helpful indicator' and 'a final and most effective check' but not a substitute for evaluating actual duties. The salary test should preserve the role of duties analysis and avoid creating a sole salary-based test—consistent with long-standing Department positions and many commenters' views.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maintain historical consistency and predictability
rubrics_metrics.description: Where possible, apply a methodology consistent with historical practice (e.g., the 2004 approach that produced a standard salary equivalent to the long-test level) to promote predictability and align with precedent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Many commenters favored the 2004/2019 methodology as consistent with historical practice and predictability. The Department notes that applying the 2004 method to contemporaneous data previously produced salary levels equivalent to the long test and promoted continuity; divergence from that endpoint (as in 2019) expanded the exemption.

rubrics_metrics.name: Legal defensibility and responsiveness to judicial precedent
rubrics_metrics.description: Select a salary methodology that is legally defensible in light of judicial decisions; avoid approaches the courts have criticized (e.g., the 2016 rule's 'untethered' methodology).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Department cited district court rulings invalidating the 2016 rule because it 'untethered the salary level test from its historical justification.' The Department therefore prefers methodologies traceable to historical practice (long-test equivalency or 2004 method) and explicitly considers legal risk when choosing percentile/region/data approaches.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider regional and industry variation if appropriate
rubrics_metrics.description: Account for differences across regions and industries when choosing a methodology (commenters suggested regional or industry-based percentiles or adjustments).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Some commenters advocated using the 2004/2019 approach (20th percentile for the South or retail industry nationally) or otherwise accounting for regional/industry differences to preserve local applicability and predictability. The Department considered these views alongside its objective to restore the screening function and to account for the one-test shift.

rubrics_metrics.name: Weigh employer burden and administrative efficiency against employee protections
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluate the size and timing of any increase in light of employer compliance burdens and the policy goal of protecting employees; recognize that many employer commenters opposed large or rapid increases even when accepting the salary test's continued existence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Commenters often opposed the proposed increase due to potential employer impacts; others acknowledged the salary-level test's utility (simplicity/'bright line') in saving administrative time. The Department notes these tradeoffs and frames protective impacts as byproducts rather than the statutory justification for the level chosen.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use an updating mechanism to reflect earnings growth
rubrics_metrics.description: Implement a mechanism to update the standard salary level periodically to account for earnings growth since the prior rule (e.g., since 2019).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Department's goal in the rulemaking includes updating the single standard salary level to account for earnings growth through an updating mechanism. This maintains relevance over time and avoids long dormancy that undermines the long-test screening function.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance precision with administrability (efficiency vs nuance)
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognize that restoring finer protections (e.g., limits on nonexempt work) increases precision but reduces administrative efficiency; a one-test system requires tradeoffs between nuance and a familiar single test.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The two-test system had four adjustable variables allowing finer calibration (two salary levels and two duties tests); a one-test system necessarily yields less nuance. The Department considered but did not propose reinstating the long duties test; it highlighted that reinstating a more rigorous duties limit could better protect lower-paid employees but would forfeit benefits of a single familiar test.
